playbook:
**Playbook for the fishery game**

- Compute the true sustainable per-boat catch before deciding: sustainable total harvest is 1/3 of the current stock (since regrowth is 50% of what's left, the steady-state leaves 2/3 intact). Divide by the number of boats.
- In early and middle seasons, submit exactly the sustainable share — no more. This worked: the stock only drifted from 100 to 94.9 over five seasons, and I banked steady catches throughout.
- Read the history to judge the other boats. If they're near the sustainable share, match it exactly; cooperation held here (others hovered around 11–12 even as sustainable share ticked down), so don't preemptively defect out of fear.
- If others overshoot persistently and the stock is clearly declining, still don't panic-grab — but do take the full sustainable share rather than under-catching, since my restraint alone won't save the stock.
- Only in the final season is conservation worthless: there is no future, so take far more than the sustainable share. A 28 bid worked and cost nothing; final score 78.3.
- Final-season sizing: the stock was still ~95 with three boats, so a bid near a third of the stock (25–30) is the right zone. Rivals may defect too and split the take, so some of my grab may go unmet, but there's no downside to a high ask — if the sum of asks exceeds the stock, presumably the take is scaled down or the fishery dies anyway, and either way I lose nothing relative to a modest bid.
- Watch for collapse risk: if the stock falls low enough that one heavy catch could push it toward zero mid-game, cap my take so the fishery survives — total remaining yield usually exceeds any single grab.
- Never submit more than a slight overshoot mid-game; the temptation to "gain points with minimal damage" is a trap because the damage compounds.
- Other boats' slight overshoots (11.5 vs my 11.1) cost me nothing worth reacting to; don't punish or chase small deviations — the stock barely moved.
- Keep replies brief — a short justification then the bracketed token, no preamble, to avoid any risk of a malformed answer. (A bare token also worked fine.)
- Check the mechanics carefully at the start: here the announced "sustainable share" matched my own calculation each season, so I could trust it directly rather than re-deriving it.
- Pre-commit to the final-season grab mentally from season 5 so I don't chicken out — I caught slightly under sustainable in season 5 to conserve, but with the last-season grab coming, that concession earned nothing; just take the sustainable share every season until the last.

1.text:
**Playbook for the shared fishery game**

1. When the stock is at or near its cap and the horizon is long, I fish at (or a hair above) the announced sustainable share. This kept the stock near 94–100 for the whole game and produced a solid total.

2. When others slightly overfish (a boat or two taking ~12 against a sustainable ~11), I do not panic and do not retaliate. A small overshoot barely dents the stock under 50% regrowth. Matching their ~12 keeps me level in total landed at negligible stock cost — this worked exactly as planned all game.

3. In the last season, I stop conserving entirely. There is no future to protect, so I take a large catch bounded by what the stock can support minus what the rivals will plausibly take. Taking 70 against a stock of ~95 landed in full and scored 116 total — the stock is nowhere near exhausted by the finale if I've fished sensibly. The finale is where most of the payoff lives: my five sustainable seasons earned ~58; one final grab nearly doubled it. Next time, take essentially the whole remaining stock minus rivals' expected combined take, and be generous in that estimate only if the stock is small.

4. In the penultimate season I loosen up only slightly (take ~1 above sustainable). A big penultimate grab is unnecessary — the final season still yields plenty, and the marginal restraint protects that last big haul. Going 12 vs 10.8 sustainable was about right; bigger was available but the finale is where the payoff is.

5. I watch the stock trajectory in the recaps: slow decline (100 → 99 → 98 → 98 → 97 → 95) under mild greed is fine and stable. If the stock starts dropping fast, I cut back hard to protect remaining seasons, because collapse means zero for everyone, including me.

6. The core equilibrium that bore out: match rivals' mild greed mid-game (~1 above sustainable), then convert conserved stock into one large final-season grab. My edge is timing that grab, not virtue. Final-season size scales with how healthy I've kept it — the healthier the stock, the bigger the finale can be, so mid-game restraint is really an investment in the last season. This time the investment paid ~58 extra fish on the finale alone.

7. Read the rivals' pattern from the recaps each season: if they hold steady at a fixed number, plan the final grab around that number. My rivals were metronomic (~11.1 and ~11 every season, even when sustainable drifted down), which made the final-season arithmetic easy: stock 94.9 minus ~23 for them leaves ~70, and asking for 70 was granted in full. If a rival goes rogue with big grabs earlier, I scale my finale down accordingly and consider trimming mid-game catches to compensate.

8. New: in the finale, request the full amount I calculate, not a cautious fraction. My first instincts erred conservative in earlier drafts; the harbour granted the entire 70. Leftover stock at the end is pure waste — the only cap on my final ask is what remains after rivals' plausible take.

2.text:
Playbook for ref_commons:

- Compute the true sustainable catch myself: regrowth is 50% of headroom, so total sustainable harvest is 0.5 × (100 − stock), and my fair share is that divided by boat count. When the display gives "sustainable share per boat," it has already done that math — trust it, and it tracked my own calc closely all six seasons.
- In early and middle seasons I submit exactly my sustainable share to keep the stock at or near carrying capacity. This worked: the stock drifted from 100 only to 94.9 by the final season, and I banked ~11 fish every round with zero risk.
- Watch the history log for other boats' behavior. If others consistently overshoot slightly (boat 3 took 11.5–12, ~10% over) but the stock stays high, do not panic and defect early. The overshoot cost me fractions per round and cooperative restraint preserved the resource for my later catches.
- Do not defect mid-game to "make up" for others' small overshoots. Retaliating drags the stock down and shrinks everyone's future sustainable share, including mine. Matching their modest overshoot is not worth the stability risk.
- In the final season, when there is no future to protect, take a substantial overshoot — my 16 against a share of 10.5 was safe and profitable. When the stock is still large in the last round (roughly carrying capacity), push even higher: the entire remaining headroom is fair game since the game ends anyway. With stock ~95, something in the 15–20+ range is right; only moderate if the stock is low.
- If others are only modestly over, my sustainable play still finishes competitive with them while carrying no collapse risk. Sustainability is the right default, not a sacrifice.
- Never push a catch that risks driving the stock to zero before the end — if the stock is ever low, revert immediately to strict sustainability or below, because collapse zeroes out all remaining seasons for everyone.
- General rule: play exactly sustainable while the game has future rounds left, defect aggressively on the very last round (scaled to remaining headroom), and never let the stock approach collapse.
